Prior hepatic encephalopathy episode 6 months ago (resolved with lactulose)

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 11 (E3V4M4). Confused, disoriented to date and year. Knows her name and that she is in a hospital. Speech is slow and dysarthric. Asterixis present bilaterally. Unable to perform number connection test.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. No ptosis. Extraocular movements intact. No facial asymmetry. Gag intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Decreased tone globally. Moves all extremities. No focal weakness.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch grossly. Unable to cooperate with formal testing.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout, symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing.
neurological_exam.gait: Not tested — too confused and at fall risk.
neurological_exam.additional: Scleral icterus. Mild jaundice. Abdomen distended with ascites (shifting dullness positive). Lower extremity pitting edema 2+ bilateral.

patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old woman with known NASH cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after two days of worsening confusion and slurred speech. Her daughter reports that the patient had been complaining of increased abdominal distension and had called her primary care provider about it three days ago. She had been told to increase her furosemide dose from 40 mg to 80 mg per day on her own, which she did. Over the following two days, she became progressively more confused, sleeping most of the day, mixing up names of grandchildren, and leaving the stove on twice. On the morning of admission, she called her daughter by the wrong name and did not recognize her son-in-law. She denied headache, fever, vision changes, or weakness. She denied chest pain or shortness of breath. She had been compliant with lactulose and rifaximin until two days ago when her daughter noticed she had forgotten multiple doses of lactulose. Her last bowel movement was two days ago. She had no recent travel, sick contacts, or dietary changes. She had been eating less than usual over the past week due to nausea. She has no history of seizures or alcohol use. Her prior hepatic encephalopathy episode six months ago had resolved with lactulose optimization over 48 hours. On review of her recent labs from one week prior, her potassium was borderline low at 3.4 mEq/L, and her creatinine was at her baseline of 1.0 mg/dL. Her family denies any falls, head trauma, or new medications.

interactions: Metformin + hepatic encephalopathy: increased risk of lactic acidosis if liver failure worsens
Metformin is renally cleared — creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (eGFR ~47 mL/min) is borderline for dose adjustment
contraindications: HOLD metformin if creatinine rises above 1.4 mg/dL (eGFR <45) or if contrast study ordered
HOLD metformin in acute illness with risk of hemodynamic instability
warnings: Current lactate 1.9 mmol/L is normal but monitor — metformin lactic acidosis risk if condition deteriorates
Recommend holding metformin during acute HE episode and restarting when metabolically stable
alternatives: Insulin sliding scale for glycemic control during acute HE episode

findings.morphology: Less frequent triphasic bursts — now isolated rather than runs

output.impression: Follow-up EEG at 36 hours shows significant improvement — triphasic waves now rare and brief, background slowing less severe. No ictal activity. NCSE excluded. Clinical correlation recommended.

abnormal_values_summary: PMN 95/mm3 — SBP excluded; diuretic-induced hypokalemia confirmed as precipitant

additional_observations: No FLAIR signal abnormality in mammillary bodies or periaqueductal gray — no Wernicke pattern
output.impression: No acute findings. No DWI restriction, no acute ischemia. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Reduce furosemide back to 40mg daily and optimize spironolactone dosing given hypokalemia precipitated HE
interactions: Furosemide + spironolactone: complementary diuretics; spironolactone is potassium-sparing and should be used to counteract furosemide-induced hypokalemia
Loop diuretic escalation without potassium supplementation precipitated hypokalemia and HE in this patient
contraindications: Do NOT increase furosemide without ensuring adequate potassium supplementation in cirrhotic patients on lactulose/rifaximin
warnings: Target weight loss with diuretics in cirrhosis: 0.5 kg/day (ascites only) or 1 kg/day (ascites + edema)
Monitor potassium closely with any diuretic adjustment
Consider oral KCl supplementation if diuretics cannot be adequately reduced
alternatives: Consider tolvaptan for sodium correction if hyponatremia persists despite diuretic optimization

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, Grade 2, precipitated by hypokalemia (iatrogenic from excess furosemide) and lactulose non-compliance

differential.key_features: Creatinine only 1.3 (baseline 1.0 — mild pre-renal); ammonia 112 umol/L strongly points to hepatic cause; no renal failure history
Na 134 mEq/L — too mild to cause encephalopathy alone; contributes marginally but HE is primary
Lactate 1.9 mmol/L normal; metformin does not directly cause encephalopathy without lactic acidosis
CT head normal; no trauma history; coagulopathy present but no clinical signs of herniation or focal deficit
No heavy alcohol history; normal nutrition overall; MRI shows no mammillary body signal; ophthalmoplegia absent

optimal_actions.action: CT head to exclude structural cause
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal CT head — no hemorrhage, infarct, or mass

optimal_actions.action: Order stat labs: ammonia, CBC, CMP with potassium, LFTs, coagulation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 112 umol/L; hypokalemia (K 2.9) from excess furosemide identified as key precipitant

optimal_actions.action: Perform EEG to confirm HE pattern and exclude NCSE
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Triphasic waves with theta-delta slowing — metabolic encephalopathy consistent with HE

optimal_actions.action: Administer IV potassium chloride to correct hypokalemia (K 2.9 → target >3.5 mEq/L)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Potassium normalizes; ammonia production from renal ammoniogenesis decreases

optimal_actions.action: Optimize lactulose: 30mL q4-6h until 2-3 soft stools/day; continue rifaximin 550mg BID
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia trending down with adequate bowel function

optimal_actions.action: Hold metformin during acute HE episode; use insulin sliding scale for glycemic control
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Metformin held appropriately — restart after metabolic stabilization

optimal_actions.action: Reduce furosemide to 40mg daily; do NOT increase diuretics without potassium supplementation in cirrhosis
Perform diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP (ascites present even without fever)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: PMN 95/mm3 — SBP excluded; portal hypertension etiology confirmed

critical_actions: Identify and correct hypokalemia (K 2.9 mEq/L) — KEY precipitant driving ammonia production
Reduce furosemide to prior dose — iatrogenic hypokalemia from dose increase was the precipitant
Optimize lactulose (patient had missed doses with resulting constipation)
CT head to exclude structural cause
EEG to confirm HE and exclude NCSE
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP (even though no fever — SBP can present without fever)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT increase furosemide further — caused hypokalemia that precipitated this HE episode
Do NOT continue metformin in acute HE with creatinine elevation above baseline
Do NOT give benzodiazepines for sedation — worsens HE
Do NOT rapidly correct hyponatremia (Na 134 — no treatment needed at this level)
key_reasoning_points: Iatrogenic hypokalemia (K 2.9 mEq/L) from increased furosemide dose is the primary identified precipitant — hypokalemia increases renal ammonia production
Missed lactulose doses with constipation (last BM 2 days ago) compounded ammonia accumulation
EEG triphasic waves confirm metabolic (hepatic) encephalopathy — triphasic waves correlate with ammonia level in HE
CT head normal excludes structural cause — metabolic workup should always follow normal CT in cirrhotic patients with encephalopathy
Metformin should be held during acute HE in a cirrhotic patient with worsening renal function due to lactic acidosis risk
SBP can present without fever — diagnostic paracentesis indicated in all cirrhotic patients with ascites presenting with encephalopathy
Hypokalemia correction is as important as lactulose in treating HE when hypokalemia is the precipitant

red_herrings.data_point: Glucose 188 mg/dL and metformin on medication list
red_herrings.intended_effect: Clinician may attribute confusion partly to hyperglycemia or suspect metformin lactic acidosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lactate is normal (1.9 mmol/L); hyperglycemia is mild and unlikely to cause encephalopathy at this level; hypokalemia and hyperammonemia are the primary drivers
